input.content:
Use ← → to navigate
A Musical Journey

The History of
Jazz

From the streets of New Orleans to concert halls around the world — the story of America's most original art form.

Ten slides · Roughly a century and a half of sound
02
An American Original

What Is Jazz?

Jazz is a music built on freedom and conversation. It blends African American blues and ragtime with European harmony, then pushes beyond both through swing, improvisation, and spontaneous interplay.

  • Improvisation — the performance is created in the moment
  • Swing — a rhythmic feel that makes the music move and dance
  • Blues — expressive notes, bent pitches, and a call-and-response spirit
  • Syncopation — accents on the unexpected beat
03
The Roots · Before 1900

Ragtime, Blues & Brass Bands

Jazz grew from a meeting of traditions in the American South and Midwest.

  • Ragtime — Scott Joplin's syncopated piano pieces gave jazz its rhythmic skeleton.
  • Blues — field hollers, spirituals, and the 12-bar blues brought emotional depth and bent notes.
  • Brass & marching bands — parades and funerals in New Orleans trained musicians in horns and collective playing.
  • Creole culture — a mix of African, French, Spanish, and Caribbean influences shaped the city's sound.
04
The Birth · New Orleans, c. 1900–1917

Where Jazz Began

In the lively neighborhoods of New Orleans, musicians began bending marches and ragtime into something looser and more expressive. Storyville's clubs and neighborhood parades became its first stages.

  • Buddy Bolden — an early cornetist often called the first jazz musician.
  • Creole jazz — clarinetists like Sidney Bechet brought virtuosic, blues-inflected solos.
  • Collective improvisation — several players weaving melodies at once, the hallmark of early jazz.
"Jazz was born in New Orleans, but its parents came from Africa."— Traditional saying
05
The Jazz Age · 1920s

Jazz Goes Global

The recording industry and the "Roaring Twenties" carried jazz from New Orleans to Chicago, New York, and Europe. The soloist became the star.

  • Louis Armstrong — virtuosic trumpet and scat singing; made the solo improviser central.
  • The Hot Fives and Sevens — his groundbreaking recordings redefined jazz soloing.
  • Dixieland & Chicago style — lively ensemble playing spread through clubs and records.
  • Jazz became the soundtrack of the "Jazz Age," tied to flappers, dances, and a new youth culture.
06
The Swing Era · 1930s–Early 1940s

The Age of Big Bands

Swing made jazz the most popular music in America. Large orchestras played arranged music built for dancing, with sections of trumpets, trombones, saxophones, and rhythm.

  • Duke Ellington — composed sophisticated, elegant works tailored to his orchestra's unique voices.
  • Count Basie — driving, riff-based swing and the "All-American Rhythm Section."
  • Benny Goodman — the "King of Swing" brought jazz to mass audiences on radio and records.
  • Billie Holiday & Ella Fitzgerald — transformed jazz singing with phrasing and emotional nuance.
07
The Revolution · Mid-1940s

Bebop — Jazz as Art

A new generation pushed back against dance-oriented swing, creating fast, complex music meant for listening — not dancing. Bebop shifted jazz from popular entertainment toward a virtuoso art form.

  • Charlie "Bird" Parker — alto saxophone genius of blistering speed and harmonic invention.
  • Dizzy Gillespie — trumpet virtuoso and bebop's charismatic ambassador.
  • Thelonious Monk — eccentric piano and compositions full of surprising angles.
  • Complex chords, rapid tempos, and daring improvisation became the new language.
08
New Directions · 1950s

Cool Jazz & Hard Bop

After bebop, jazz split into contrasting moods — a calm, controlled "cool" and a RETURN to bluesy, gospel-rooted intensity.

  • Miles Davis — "Birth of the Cool" and later the spare, haunting "Kind of Blue" (1959).
  • Modal jazz — improvisation over scales instead of fast chord changes, giving players more space.
  • Hard bop — Art Blakey, Horace Silver, and others brought blues, gospel, and soul back in.
  • John Coltrane — emerged as a towering saxophonist searching for new spiritual depths.
09
Breaking Boundaries · 1960s–1970s

Free Jazz & Fusion

Jazz grew more experimental, abandoning traditional structures and embracing electricity, rock, and global rhythms.

  • Free jazz — Ornette Coleman and John Coltrane's "A Love Supreme" explored freedom and spirituality.
  • Jazz fusion — Miles Davis's "Bitches Brew" mixed jazz improvisation with rock and electric instruments.
  • Weather Report & Herbie Hancock — keyboards and synthesizers opened vast new sonic worlds.
  • Jazz-rock, funk, and world influences widened the music's audience and vocabulary.
10
The Legacy · Today & Beyond

Jazz Lives On

Jazz is no longer only an American music — it is a worldwide language. It keeps reinventing itself while honoring the giants who came before.

  • Modern artists like Wynton Marsalis, Kamasi Washington, and Esperanza Spalding carry the tradition forward.
  • Jazz education, festivals, and archives preserve its history for new generations.
  • Hip-hop, neo-soul, and electronic music continue to borrow from jazz's spirit of improvisation.
  • Its core idea endures: listen, respond, and create something new in the moment.
"Jazz is the freedom to be yourself, together."— The enduring spirit of jazz
